children.name: Special Education and Accessibility
children.blurb: A review of research on AI with students with disabilities found something uncomfortable. Much of the work described AI as a way to relieve adults of the burden of working with these students, rather than as a way to empower the students and their families (Rice, 2023).

children.name: English Learners and Newcomers
children.blurb: In a trial with 217 second graders learning English, most of them Latino, a computer tutor taught the vocabulary of science and social studies units. Students who used it learned more of the taught words than students who did not, with an effect of 0.38 (Baker et al., 2020).

children.name: Communicating With Families
children.blurb: A school district once had a problem with truancy notices. The letters sent to families were written in legal language, warning of consequences and citing the education code.

children.name: Wellbeing, Behavior, Attendance, and Safety
children.blurb: A study of 14 companies that monitor students online found that most watch students around the clock, not just during school hours. Most use AI to flag concerning content, but fewer than half described any human review of those flags.

children.name: Counseling, College, and Career
children.blurb: Every spring, many high school graduates are admitted to college, plan to go, and never show up in the fall. Researchers call this summer melt.

sections.body: This part of school life covers the students and families who most need careful attention, including special education and accessibility, English learners and newcomers, communication with families, wellbeing and safety, and counseling and college. AI in these areas is described as supporting the work around these students rather than replacing the people who know them. The book presents this part as holding some of the strongest evidence in the Volume, with several randomized trials involving messages to families and support for students after high school. It also treats these chapters as places where the firmest rules about decisions that must stay with people apply.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: What works in this part is careful attention to the students and families who need it most, and the book points to randomized trials involving messages to families and support for students after high school as some of its strongest evidence. What does not work is letting AI take over decisions that must stay with people, and the book holds firmly to that rule across these chapters. The rule it holds to is that these decisions remain human, even where AI can help with communication and support. The book treats this part as both evidence rich and rule bound, so the promise and the limits sit together.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages fit together as five connected areas of student and family life, each with its own focus. Special Education and Accessibility and English Learners and Newcomers cover the students who need particular care and the supports around them. Communicating With Families is where the randomized trials on messages to families appear, and it connects the school to the home. Wellbeing, Behavior, Attendance, and Safety covers the daily conditions that let students stay present and safe. Counseling, College, and Career covers the path after high school, where the book also finds strong trial evidence. A teacher would go to the first two for classroom and language support, a leader to communication and wellbeing for school wide practice, and a parent to counseling and college for what comes next.
